I'm very happy, privileged to open the special focus session, Innovation in Education, EdTech, AI, and the Learning Revolution, from Promise to Proof. Executive Director Russell, Minister Ratnik, Minister Abdel Latif, distinguished colleagues, partners, educators, young people, and friends, again, warm welcome and thank you for joining us for this special focus session conducted indeed in very close cooperation between UNICEF and Estonia. The new global learning crisis is affecting education systems and schools around the world as we speak. On average, seven out of 10 children cannot read a simple sentence these days. It is becoming increasingly difficult to bring young people into classroom that in many respects still resemble a relic of industrial age. Learning outcomes remain fragile while education continues to suffer from underinvestment. To turn the tide, we need something bold, perhaps even revolutionary. Is AI the answer? We don't know yet. AI is developing at extraordinary speed, much faster than governments can regulate it and much faster than education systems can adapt it. And that is understandable. By the very nature, both regulation and education require caution, evidence, and time. When children are involved, risk must be carefully accessed and mitigated. Speed cannot replace judgment, evidence, or responsibility. But the question is, can we afford not to try AI in education? I believe the answer is no. Frankly, when I went to school, I did not know how to read properly and my math was really embryonic. And that was precisely the reason, frankly, why kids were going to school, to learn to read, write, and calculate. My children, however, had to take a test demonstrating their reading and mathematical skills just to enter the first grade. I think it's frankly ridiculous, but This is a reality. And now I have witnessed how quickly youngsters embrace AI. They turned to agents while I was still reflecting which model to use. So we should ask ourselves, how have we been able to equip them to use AI critically, safely, creatively, and how we equip the teachers to guide them in this new AI-enabled world? This is also a question I have been reflecting on under my second hat as a co-chair of a first global UN dialogue on AI governance. One lesson from that process is very, very clear. Global discussions on AI become meaningful for people only when they address their real needs and their everyday lives. Few places make that connection more tangible than the good old classroom. which itself, of course, needs to undergo, if not a total transformation, then at least a solid facelift. One thing is certain, no government, UN agency, education system, or technology company can address this challenge alone. So we need teachers, young people, governments, researchers, the private sector, and organizations such as UNICEF around the same table. Estonia's experience tells us that digital transformation in education is not primarily about devices, technology, software. It is about people, trust, and long-term choices. It means investing in teachers, building digital and AI skills, creating the right infrastructure, giving schools the opportunity to experiment, learn, and innovate. And the main goal of Estonia's AI Leap program is not to replace teachers with AI, nor to put AI into classrooms for its own sake. It is about helping teachers rethink how they teach using technology, building their own AI literacy, and strengthening students' thinking and learning skills through the purposeful use of AI. Today, we will hear about the first results of this ambitious project. But Estonia is not here to present one national model as a universal answer. Contexts differ and what works in one country, frankly, may not work in our context. So that is why I'm really very happy and pleased that today's discussion brings together such different perspectives. On the second side, what we want is to share our experience with our global partners, including under the UN roof, to exchange best practices and to learn from all of you. as we work together to address the learning crisis. So from promise to proof, for me, means sharing our practical experience, including what works, what does not work, what still requires further evidence, and what may already be useful to adapt elsewhere. Let us hope that this conversation makes a real difference. With that, I'm honored to hand over to Edie Russell for her statement.

Well, thank you so much, Mr. President, and thank you for your leadership on this issue. I think, you know, I say this all the time, but we have hundreds of millions of children who are out of school in the world, and we have millions more who are in school and not learning. Everyone needs to worry about that because what happens to those kids, what happens to those communities, those societies? At the same time, we have artificial intelligence and other digital technologies developing at extraordinary speed. But I think the important thing in my mind here is that technology is not an easy fix to these very big problems. Simply putting new technology into a classroom doesn't make it an educational innovation. UNICEF's new strategic plan recognizes that digital technologies and innovation, when deployed equitably and based on evidence, will be increasingly important to how we deliver results for every child. Our role here is to help connect global ambition and innovation with what works in classrooms and communities. That means asking some very basic questions. Does technology improve learning? Can teachers use it effectively? Do they know how to use it effectively? Can it work at scale, including countries and communities with limited connectivity and resources? And we deal with that problem a lot. You know, there are many places where The idea of connecting to the Internet is almost inconceivable. Does it reach children who are most likely to be left behind? And does it protect children's rights, privacy, safety, and well-being? AI is moving at lightning speed. The goal is quite straightforward, to ensure that AI expands learning opportunities for all children, particularly those too often left behind while safeguarding their rights, safety, and well-being. To achieve that, we believe action is needed in three areas. First, we need standards so that governments and education systems can identify effective, responsible solutions and take them to scale. Second, we need sustainable financing so the benefits of innovation are not reserved for children in the wealthiest countries or communities alone. And third, we need a broader movement, bringing together governments, educators, technology leaders, researchers, civil society, and young people to build trust, strengthen political will, and turn principles into action. So today, we invite all of you to help define the compact's priorities and direction. We are at the dawn of a new technological age. Whether it will benefit or harm children is really up to all of us. We look forward to working together to ensure that the AI revolution becomes a learning revolution for every single child. Thank you very much.

We can't just meet some children at some point in time with some money. We should be for every child. Would you be willing to take a part of your contribution to a thematic fund? so that on the issue you care about, we can also meet the needs of children beyond where your customers or your supply chain is. And we have seen a resounding response and buy-in. It's one part of why our private sector RR has also gone up in core and thematic. On thematic, I mean, thematic is by design earmarked by the thematic area, but not by countries or tightly projectized. It's exactly why it is so flexible, and we very much hope to see more contributions to the thematic funds. Thank you, Madam President, distinguished members of the Executive Board. It is my honor to introduce the UNICEF Strategic Plan, updated financial estimates for 2026 to 2029. When we presented the integrated budget one year ago, UNICEF was already confronting a rapidly changing financing environment. Today, these pressures remain significant. Declining official development assistance, fiscal constraints, and geopolitical uncertainty continue to affect both the level and predictability of resources available for children, as noted in the previous session. Against this backdrop, UNICEF continues to take a prudent and conservative approach to financial planning. Total income for 2026 is projected at 6.46 billion, 20% below the 2025 actual level, and it is expected to remain broadly stable throughout the remainder of the strategic plan period. While the overall funding outlook is challenging, the continued downward trend in regular resources is particularly alarming. These are UNICEF's most flexible funds, allowing us to direct resources where needs are greatest, sustain programs in underfunded contexts, and respond rapidly to emerging crises, as illustrated in the previous session. Protecting and expanding flexible, predictable, and multi-year funding, therefore, remains very critical. At the same time, UNICEF is adapting. Planned expenditure is being aligned with the lower income outlook, while we continue to prioritize program delivery and maintain prudent liquidity. The Future Focus initiative is advancing organizational efficiencies and helping UNICEF operate more sustainably within this constrained financial environment. Importantly, even as resources become more constrained, we must preserve the viability of our country programs. We are therefore proposing to increase the minimum annual regular resource allocation for each country program from 850,000 to 1.1 million beginning in 2027. This reflects the cumulative inflation since the minimum was last adjusted in 2013. UNICEF will continue to closely monitor income, expenditure, and financial risks, and adjust our plans as necessary while keeping the Executive Board informed. We remain deeply grateful to Member States and all our partners for their continued support.
